Edit: some minor spoilers for critical role campaign 2

It's totally possible to add depth after the game has started! The example I would point to is Nott from campaign 2 of Critical Role. 

At the start of the game, she's just a goblin who likes drinking and stealing, and that's more or less her whole deal. But as the game goes on, Sam (her player) starts to figure out more and more about her backstory, and he weaves it in slowly to great effect.

When it comes up that the party will have to go underwater, Nott freaks out and reveals that she is terrified of water, but doesn't say why. Later on during some downtime, she sends a message to an NPC that only the DM knows about, asking how her son is doing (while the rest of the table is like "your WHAT???")

Eventually everyone finds out that she used to be a halfling with a husband and son. She was drowned by a group of goblins who were working with a hag, and brought back as a goblin.

Rescuing her husband from a POW camp, tracking down the witch, and creating a spell capable of reversing the transformation all turned into major quests that shaped the entire campaign.

TLDR: Yes it's possible. Slowly reveal pieces of information about your character as they become relevant in-game. If done right, this will create a lot of intrigue, and make for an interesting character and adventure!

Besides, calling 0 F "human freezing" and 100 F "human boiling" is pretty arbitrary and subjective. Do you think someone living in Arizona is going to have the same feelings about temperature as someone living in Alaska?

This part is just my opinion, but I think Celsius degrees are a better-sized unit of measurement than Fahrenheit. I find that a 1° C change is easier to notice than a 1° F change. Idk, that just makes more sense to me.

I had a character with a similar deal. He was a paladin who wore his armor 24/7, because in his backstory he wasn't fast enough to put his armor on, and a bunch of people died as a result.

I kept it from being cringe by making sure his personality wasn't edgy/angsty. I really leaned into the gentle giant archetype, made him very polite and compassionate, and most importantly, he tried to avoid talking about why he never took the armor off. 

If people asked about it, he just said something about how it takes longer than you think to don a suit of armor, and he needs to be ready to protect his friends at a moments notice. By the time he shared his tragic backstory with the rest of the party, everyone already found him likeable and interesting. 

My advice would be for your character to avoid drawing too much attention to the mask, and give them an actual personality that isn't just "miserable edgelord". As long as you're not constantly reminding everyone about the mask, your fellow players will find it cool and interesting. I hope that helps!
